To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the warm-up protocol did not influence VO2, heart rate or performance time in the standardized or tethered swim, but did influence blood lactate accumulation.
the high-intensity warm-up resulted in higher blood lactate levels, higher oxygen uptake, higher heart rate, and lower swimming performance than the low-intensity warm up.

(1) the high-intensity warm-up protocol was more effective than the other warm-up conditions at increasing blood lactate concentration, heart rate, and oxygen uptake during a standardized freestyle swim; (2) there was no difference in performance between the three warm-up conditions during the 183-m swim at 110% VO(2max) and (3), the high-intensity and low-intensity protocols did not differ in the time to exhaustion during a tethered swim.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the effects of high-intensity warm-up and low-intensity exercise on physiological responses, and on the performance of high-intensity freestyling and tethered swimming.
the effects of high and low-intensity aerobic warm-up on physiological responses and performance.
the effects of high and low intensity warm-ups on physiological and performance responses.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the warm-up protocol did not affect the performance times in the standardized and tethering swim tests and did not affect the lactate accumulation after the warm-ups and the standardized and the tethered swimming tests.
the warm-up protocol did not have a significant effect on performance.

the warm-up protocol did not affect the physiological responses to the standardized swim or tethered swim, but the HWU did increase blood lactate levels after the warm-up, the standardized swim, and the tethered swim.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

a low intensity warm-up (LWU), consisting of 366 m at 70% of maximal oxygen uptake, is as effective as a high intensity warm-up (HWU), consisting of four 46 m sprints at 1 minute intervals at 110% maximal oxygen uptake, for increasing performance in a standardized 183 m freestyle swim at 110% of VO2 max and for improving performance in tethered swimming.
a warm up is necessary to improve swimming performance.
a low-intensity warm up (70% VO2max) prior to a 110% VO 2max freestyle swim resulted in lower blood lactate levels and higher VO2 levels than a no warm-up condition.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a high-intensity warm-up is not detrimental to performance in the standardized swim and tether swim.
warm-up intensity is a key variable that can influence physiological responses and performance in high-intensity exercise.
a warm-up that includes a 366-m freestyle swim at 70-75% VO2max followed by four 46-m sprints at 110% VO 2 max is effective at improving the high-intensity performance of swimmers.
